findings.title: No ratchet gate against select(*) over-fetch recurrence
findings.principle: Every new or edited Supabase query in app/api and lib must name its selected columns explicitly. A CI job counts occurrences of select("*") / select('*') under app/api and fails the build if the count exceeds the last-recorded baseline (currently 107), mirroring the existing tsc/lint ratchet already in quality.yml. A route that genuinely needs every column (an owner-only admin export) is added to a small, named allowlist file with a one-line reason, never silently exempted.
findings.why: select(*) is Solen's single most repeated performance-and-security bug shape. The SWEEP audit independently found and fixed the identical over-fetch pattern on at least 5 separate routes, each time re-discovered by a human or agent reading code rather than caught mechanically. Without a standing count, a new route or an edit to an old one can silently reintroduce the exact bug class that was already paid down once.
findings.local_evidence: grep -rn 'select("\*"' app/api --include=*.ts (and the single-quote variant) currently returns 107 hits across app/api, even though _plans/SWEEP_BACKLOG.md records the identical bug independently found and fixed on app/api/salons/route.ts, app/api/salons/[slug]/route.ts, app/api/bookings/route.ts, app/api/profile/favorites/route.ts, and app/api/availability/[salon_id]/route.ts (lines 8, 18-19, 47-48, 50, all marked STALE-FIXED/FIXED).
findings.absence_proof: grep -rln 'select("\*"\|select \*\|overfetch\|over-fetch\|select-star' scripts .claude/hooks -> only scripts/db-backup-kill-test.ts and scripts/ring8b-kill-test.ts matched, both unrelated kill-test scripts, not a gate. grep -rn lighthouse .github/workflows/*.yml and grep for select-star patterns in .github/workflows/*.yml both return nothing. transactions-concurrency.md and caching.md name the anti-pattern in prose but propose no counter or CI check.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/transactions-concurrency.md:565 names 'explicit narrow column list (not *)' as the T1-recommended pattern, and SWEEP_BACKLOG.md documents past fixes, but neither is a standing, re-checked gate; both are one-time narrative records of a problem already fixed once.
findings.where_it_should_live: a new job in .github/workflows/quality.yml (same ratchet shape as the existing tsc/lint jobs) plus, once written, a line in _backend-system/LAW.md naming the baseline count and the allowlist file path.
findings.enforcement: gate: select-star-ratchet (grep count vs a committed baseline file, fails the build if the count increases; a companion allowlist file for legitimately full-row admin/service-role reads)

findings.title: The one performance budget that exists (LCP) is documented but never enforced in CI, and INP/CLS/bundle have no number at all
findings.principle: Every customer-facing route's performance budget is a number checked by a machine, not a manual step in a design-wave checklist: LCP <= 2.5s (p75, mobile), INP <= 200ms (p75), CLS <= 0.1 (p75), matching Google's Core Web Vitals 'good' thresholds (web.dev), each captured by an automated Lighthouse CI run against the built app for a small named set of representative routes (home, /[city]/[category], salon PDP, booking flow), with the report archived so a regression is diffable against the prior run, not dependent on a human's memory of a manual check.
findings.why: A budget nobody's CI enforces decays the moment the person who ran the manual Lighthouse check moves to the next task; performance regressions stay invisible until a user complains, by which point the causal commit is long gone. LCP correlates with meaningfully lower conversion when slow, per web.dev's own case-study aggregation already cited in this repo's own psychology research, so this is not a cosmetic metric to leave unenforced.
findings.local_evidence: _design-system/WORK_TYPES.md:282 and WAVE_PLAN.md:86,89,137 and LOCKFILE.md:990,1028 all state 'LCP <=2.5s' with Tool listed as 'Lighthouse CLI or Chrome DevTools', a manual instruction, scoped to per-wave design verification of customer screens, not to every PR or every route. grep for 'lighthouse' across scripts/ and .github/ returns zero hits, confirming no automation ever runs it.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rniE '\bLCP\b|\bINP\b|\bCLS\b|web vital|core web vital' across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, _design-system, CLAUDE.md found LCP only inside design-system wave-verification docs and never as a CI-checked number; INP appears only in RATIONALE.md/PSYCHOLOGY.md as a motion-timing citation (<=200ms for interaction feedback), never as a page-performance budget; find . -iname '*lighthouse*' -not -path '*/node_modules/*' returned nothing; grep -rn lighthouse .github/workflows/*.yml returned nothing.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the LCP number (2.5s) is locked as a design-system gate for wave-based UI ships in LOCKFILE.md, but it only binds a manual verifier-agent pass during active design sweeps on customer screens, not an always-on CI check, and it does not cover routes touched outside a named 'wave.' INP and CLS have no numeric Solen-specific budget anywhere outside generic web.dev citations in research docs.
findings.where_it_should_live: a new .github/workflows/lighthouse.yml (or a step in quality.yml) running @lhci/cli against a preview build for 3-5 named routes; the existing LCP number moves from WAVE_PLAN.md into this CI config as the enforced source of truth, and INP/CLS numbers are added alongside it.
findings.enforcement: gate: lighthouse-ci (numeric thresholds per route, fails the PR on a regression past budget)

findings.title: No standing per-page query-count budget; fan-outs are only caught by after-the-fact audits
findings.principle: Every customer-facing page or API route states, in a one-line comment at its data-fetching entry point, the maximum number of sequential (non-parallelized) database round trips it is allowed to make. A page whose real requirement grows past 3 sequential round trips must either parallelize with Promise.all or collapse into one RPC before merging, not after a sweep audit finds it months later.
findings.why: Every fan-out bug the SWEEP audit fixed (inspo's 9-call mount fan-out, the PDP's triple salon query, /api/salons's serial awaits, live-state's up-to-6 sequential queries) was found by a human or agent manually reading a specific file during a scheduled audit, not by any standing check. The same shape can reappear in the next new route or the next edit to an old one with nothing catching it before ship, exactly the pattern that already recurred multiple times in one product.
findings.local_evidence: _plans/SWEEP_BACKLOG.md documents at least 4 independently-discovered fan-out/serial-query bugs (lines 10-15 for salons' serial awaits, 12-13 for inspo's 9-call fan-out, 14-15 for the PDP's triple query, 85-86 for live-state's 6 sequential queries). Verified live in this session that all are now fixed: app/[locale]/inspo/page.tsx calls a single /api/discovery/category-meta endpoint (confirmed present on disk); app/[locale]/salon/[slug]/layout.tsx uses a React cache()'d getSalonMeta shared between generateMetadata and the layout body; app/api/salons/route.ts:346 uses Promise.all. Each fix was reactive, discovered during a point-in-time audit, never prevented by a standing rule.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rniE 'query budget|per-page.*quer|round.trip.*budget' across _backend-system, _docs, CLAUDE.md returned nothing. transactions-concurrency.md discusses N+1 in prose (section 4) but names no numeric ceiling or comment convention for sequential round trips per page.
findings.existing_coverage: none as a forward-looking rule; _plans/SWEEP_BACKLOG.md is a one-time discovered-and-fixed list generated from a single audit pass, not a rule that prevents recurrence in future code.
findings.where_it_should_live: the performance section of _backend-system's eventual LAW.md, plus a one-line convention documented in _docs/BACKEND.md's data-fetching overview.
findings.enforcement: checklist (code review) today; a heuristic automated version could grep for consecutive `await supabase` calls not wrapped in Promise.all within one function body, but that has real false-positive risk, so it stays a behavioral rule and review checklist item, not a hard gate, until proven out

findings.title: No frozen trigger for when adding a cache layer is allowed; the premature-caching guidance is advisory only
findings.principle: A new caching layer (unstable_cache, a new Redis-backed cache-aside, a materialized view, or an extended CDN TTL) may only be added after the PR description states the specific measured number that justifies it: for a DB-bound case, an EXPLAIN ANALYZE execution time; for a network-bound case, a measured p95 response time from real dev or production traffic. A cache added on 'this looks like it could get slow' with no attached number gets reverted, not merged.
findings.why: Caching hides correctness bugs (staleness, an extra invalidation surface) for a benefit that only pays off once the underlying operation is actually measured to be slow. _backend-system/research/caching.md and data-modeling.md already articulate this strongly ('none are currently justified,' 'premature until measured'), but nothing stops a future session from adding a cache anyway, because the advice lives in a researched file, not a frozen law or a gate, and an added cache does not look wrong to a reviewer the way an over-fetch does; it looks like an optimization.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/research/caching.md's 'Premature at our scale' section explicitly lists distributed locking, XFetch, materialized views, and a general Redis response cache as premature, each with a named revisit trigger. This file lives under _backend-system/research/, and the orchestrator has already independently confirmed _backend-system/LAW.md does not exist on disk, so none of these named triggers are enforced law, only narrative advice a future session may or may not read.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rniE 'premature.*cach|caching.*premature|cache.*hides.*bug|hides bugs' across _backend-system, _docs, CLAUDE.md found only the caching.md/data-modeling.md prose itself, no LAW.md, no gate, no PR-template field. No .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md exists in the repo (confirmed absent when listing .github/workflows).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the reasoning and specific triggers exist in caching.md and data-modeling.md:242 ('a dedicated caching layer... is premature until a specific, measured query is shown to be a bottleneck'), but the file is unfrozen research, not enforced law, and carries no PR-facing checklist item.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md once written, cross-referenced from CLAUDE.md's fable-backend trigger list; in the short term, a checklist line in a PR template.
findings.enforcement: checklist item today ('name the measured number that justifies this cache'); not code-gateable since 'is this measured' requires human judgment, not a grep

findings.title: LCP-priority image loading was flagged twice in a dated audit and remains unfixed on the highest-traffic card component
findings.principle: The first 1-2 above-the-fold images on every list/grid page (search results, homepage rails, category browse) carry `priority` (or `fetchPriority="high"`) on their next/image element. A card component rendered in more than one context (e.g. SalonCard used in both a homepage rail and search results) accepts an explicit isAboveFold or index prop so the caller opts the first instance in; this is a checked component contract, not left to whichever page happens to remember.
findings.why: An LCP image that lazy-loads by Next's default is the most direct way to blow the LCP <=2.5s budget the design system has already locked (LOCKFILE.md:990), because the single largest, most important image on the page competes with the JS bundle for the browser's attention instead of being prioritized ahead of it.
findings.local_evidence: app/[locale]/_components/homepage/SalonCard.tsx:429 still renders its <Image> with no `priority` prop, confirmed by direct read this session. This exact gap was independently named twice in _design-system/research/PSYCH_AUDIT_2026-07-07.md:45,85 and AUDIT_CHANGELIST_2026-07-07.md:51-52,69, both dated 2026-07-07, and as of today (2026-07-26) it is still unfixed in the exact file named.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n priority on SearchTemplate.tsx and SalonCard.tsx returns zero hits for the Image priority prop (the one match found is an unrelated comment using the word 'priority' in a different context). No lint rule or gate exists in .claude/hooks or scripts for a missing priority prop on a first-rendered next/image.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the requirement is written down twice in dated audit docs (PSYCH_AUDIT_2026-07-07.md, AUDIT_CHANGELIST_2026-07-07.md) as an 'opportunity' at low/medium severity, neither ticked off, neither backed by a gate.
findings.where_it_should_live: a short line in _design-system/COMPONENT_REGISTRY.md's SalonCard entry (accept an isFirst/priority prop) plus the actual code fix in SalonCard.tsx and SearchTemplate.tsx's first-card render path.
findings.enforcement: gate: image-priority-lint (a small script/eslint rule flagging a next/image with `fill` and no `priority` inside a .map() at index 0) is the eventual target; today it is a named, still-open code fix with no gate behind it

findings.title: N+1 query risk assessment rests on a 4-file sample, not a systematic check
findings.principle: Any Supabase query issued inside a .map()/for-loop over a previously-fetched result set must either use PostgREST resource embedding (one .select() with the join expressed via foreign key) or be justified inline with a comment naming why per-row logic cannot be embedded. A lightweight repo-wide check for this shape (a loop body followed by an awaited `.from(` call) runs at least once per quarter as part of the existing sweep-backlog process, since only a 4-file sample has ever actually been read for this specific risk.
findings.why: N+1 queries scale with the length of the loop and silently multiply DB round trips under real traffic in a way a dev pass with a handful of rows will never reveal. The current confidence level (a 4-file sample) is not evidence the remaining ~165 API routes are clean; it is the audit's own admission that most of the codebase was never actually checked for this specific failure mode.
findings.local_evidence: _backend-system/audit/transactions-concurrency.md:41,265 states directly: 'The N+1/embedding check (question 6) sampled 4 files that looked... the remaining ~165 were not individually read, so a genuine N+1 could exist in an [unread file]'. This is the audit's own stated confidence level, not an outside inference about it.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rniE 'n\+1|n plus one' across scripts and .claude/hooks found zero automated checks; the term appears only in the research/audit prose files (transactions-concurrency.md), never in a script or CI job.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the risk is correctly named and the general fix (PostgREST resource embedding) is documented as T1 law in transactions-concurrency.md:565, but the audit explicitly flags its own coverage as a 4-file sample, not a systematic sweep, and no periodic re-check exists to close that gap.
findings.where_it_should_live: a scheduled quarterly item in the existing sweep-backlog generation process (_plans/SWEEP_BACKLOG.md's own P1 discovery mechanism).
findings.enforcement: checklist (periodic manual/agent sweep); a heuristic grep-based flag is feasible but will carry real false positives (not every loop-with-a-query is a bug), so full automation is not recommended until the heuristic is proven low-noise

findings.title: "Measure before, one change, measure after" binds the agent's conduct but leaves no artifact in commit or PR history
findings.principle: Every commit or PR whose description claims a performance improvement (faster, fewer queries, fewer round trips, smaller bundle) must include the actual before-number and after-number, with units, in the commit message or PR body. A performance-motivated change with no numbers attached is treated as unverified and re-measured before merge, the same way a correctness fix requires the reported bug and a reproduction.
findings.why: CLAUDE.md rule 9 already binds Claude's own conduct to measure-first performance work with a before-number and an after-number, and SWEEP_BACKLOG entries genuinely follow this well in several fix comments, but this is a rule about agent conduct inside a session, not a project convention a human contributor, a future agent session without that memory loaded, or a code reviewer can check against. A claimed optimization with no attached number is currently indistinguishable in git history from a guessed one.
findings.local_evidence: _plans/SWEEP_BACKLOG.md line 10 is a genuinely good working example ('Measured: ?category=coiffeur alone = 0.24s; +city=basel = 0.5s warm / 3.1s cold... re-measured on dev: category alone 0.20s warm...'), proving the discipline works and already paid off once. But other perf-labeled entries in the same file (e.g. line 89's [low] with_slots entry) describe the problem shape without ever attaching a measured before/after number, showing the practice is inconsistent even within one file.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rniE 'before.*number.*after.*number|measure.first|measure-first' across _backend-system and CLAUDE.md found the rule only in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (the agent-behavior layer) and ~/.claude/skills/fable-backend/SKILL.md, never in _docs/BACKEND.md, _rules/*, or any PR template (no .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md exists in the repo).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: exists as a behavioral law for the AI agent (tier 7 of the CLAUDE.md precedence chain), which is real but scoped to sessions that load that specific memory file; it is not a project-level artifact requirement that survives independent of which agent or human does the work.
findings.where_it_should_live: a .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md field ('If this PR claims a performance improvement, paste the before/after number here') so the requirement binds humans and agents alike, not only a Claude session with the right memory loaded.
findings.enforcement: doc-only convention today (PR-template checklist item); not mechanically gate-able since verifying 'is this a real number' requires human judgment

findings.title: No bundle-size budget or monitoring exists
findings.principle: The production first-load JS for each of the 3-5 highest-traffic routes (home, search results, salon PDP) is measured after every deploy and may not grow more than 10% over the last recorded baseline without an explicit PR note naming what was added and why. A bundle-analyzer report is generated in CI and the gzipped first-load JS size for those routes is the tracked, ratcheted number.
findings.why: Bundle size directly drives Time to Interactive and INP on the mid-range Android devices a Swiss mass-market booking app's actual customers likely carry. A silently growing bundle (a new heavy dependency, an un-tree-shaken import) degrades every single page load and, unlike a slow query, produces zero server-side signal to catch it: nothing errors, nothing times out, the page is simply slower for everyone with no alert firing.
findings.local_evidence: next.config.mjs:12 records exactly one deliberate bundle-size decision ever made ('B4 load win: tree-shake icon barrel... @phosphor-icons/react removed, migrated to lucide-react's Footprints'), proving the team has cared about this exactly once, reactively, with no ongoing tracking since. package.json has zero bundle-analyzer dependency (@next/bundle-analyzer or equivalent) in devDependencies.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'analyze|bundle-analyzer' package.json next.config.mjs returned nothing. grep -rniE 'query budget|performance budget|perf budget|bundle budget|bundle size' across the whole estate returned only one unquantified prose mention (_design-system/SOURCE.md:819: 'iOS Safari is the strictest perf budget. Optimize for it.', with no number, no route, no tool attached).
findings.existing_coverage: none: the single existing bundle decision (the Phosphor-icons removal) was a one-off manual observation, not a monitored, numeric, recurring budget.
findings.where_it_should_live: next.config.mjs (wire @next/bundle-analyzer behind an ANALYZE=true env flag) plus a CI step in quality.yml that runs `next build` and greps the build output's First Load JS column for the tracked routes against a committed baseline file.
findings.enforcement: gate: bundle-size-ratchet (numeric, same ratchet shape as the existing tsc/lint jobs in quality.yml)

findings.title: No timing instrumentation exists anywhere, so a slow query cannot be distinguished from a slow page or a cold start
findings.principle: Every API route handler that performs one or more DB queries logs a single structured line on completion containing at minimum: route name, total handler duration, and the summed duration of its DB calls, via a shared timing wrapper around the Supabase client call, not ad hoc per-call console.time. A request whose handler-total is high but DB-total is low is then diagnosable as a rendering/cold-start problem, and the reverse as a query problem, without a fresh, one-off investigation every single time.
findings.why: Without this split, every 'the PDP feels slow' report starts from zero: whoever investigates cannot tell from any existing signal whether the DB, a slow third-party call, a cold Lambda start, or client-side hydration is the culprit, and must instrument ad hoc, from scratch, every time. This is the literal distinction this domain's brief asks for, and today nothing in the codebase can answer it without a fresh investigation.
findings.local_evidence: grep -rn 'Server-Timing|console.time(|performance.now()' across app/api and lib returned zero matches, confirmed this session. The only per-request timing anywhere in the researched files is manual, ad hoc, and done once during a single audit (_plans/SWEEP_BACKLOG.md line 10's hand-measured curl timings), never a standing instrumentation the app itself emits on every request.
findings.absence_proof: same grep as above (0 hits across app/api and lib). reliability.md and caching.md both discuss latency extensively in prose (timeouts, p99 budgets for external dependencies) but never mention an internal per-request timing/logging convention, only external dependency latency.
findings.existing_coverage: none directly: the closest existing thing is lib/health.ts's 2-second PROBE_TIMEOUT_MS for dependency health checks, which is a liveness probe, a different concern from per-request DB-time-vs-handler-time attribution.
findings.where_it_should_live: a shared lib/db-timing.ts wrapper around the Supabase client's .select()/.rpc() calls, and a structured console.log convention (matching the project's own existing error-logging convention, '[Component] description') for the summary line at the end of each route handler.
findings.enforcement: checklist/convention today (a code-review item: 'does this new route log its DB-time vs handler-time'); could become a lint-gated requirement later (requiring the wrapper import in any file that imports the Supabase server client) once the pattern is proven out in practice

findings.title: No image weight or format budget exists as a number
findings.principle: Every salon/service/gallery photo served through next/image is capped at a maximum rendered weight of 200KB at the largest breakpoint it is displayed at (measured via next build's image-optimization report), formats default to Next's own AVIF/WebP output (no override currently disables them), and quality stays at Next's default of 75 unless a specific photo (e.g. a PDP hero) is explicitly justified at a higher number in an inline comment.
findings.why: Photos are the single largest asset on every Solen customer screen by design (the FLOORS LAW's roughly one-third photographic-area requirement, LOCKFILE.md), so an unbounded photo weight is the single biggest lever on LCP and total page weight on every discovery/PDP surface. With no number set, nobody would notice a regression (an accidentally uncompressed upload, a gallery photo served at full camera resolution) until it shows up as a slow LCP metric with no attached cause.
findings.local_evidence: next.config.mjs's `images:` block (lines 54-98) configures only `remotePatterns` (allowed hostnames), with no `formats`, `quality`, `deviceSizes`, or `imageSizes` override present, meaning Solen relies entirely on Next.js's un-pinned, un-inspected defaults for its own photo set and has never verified what those defaults actually produce.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'formats:|quality' next.config.mjs returned zero hits. grep -rniE 'image.*budget|photo.*weight|kb.*image|image.*kb' across _design-system and _backend-system returned nothing quantified; the FLOORS LAW's imagery requirement (LOCKFILE.md) specifies viewport AREA/percentage, never a byte-weight ceiling.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: LOCKFILE.md and the FLOORS LAW extensively specify photo PRESENCE and proportion (>= 1/3 viewport, largest element of every SalonCard) but never photo WEIGHT; these are visually-motivated design rules with zero overlap with a performance byte-budget.
findings.where_it_should_live: next.config.mjs (pin `images.formats` explicitly even if it matches current defaults, so a future Next major-version bump can't silently change them) plus a one-line note in _backend-system's eventual performance-law section.
findings.enforcement: doc-only threshold today; a stretch gate could check next build's image-optimization manifest against the 200KB ceiling per route, but this is a nice-to-have automation given the photo count is still small at 28 salons, not an urgent one
